1: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was the English naturalist who reshaped our understanding of life. The Origin of Species is the book in which he sets out his theory of evolution; these opening pages introduce his argument and its forerunners.
2: Plutarch (c. A.D. 46–120) was a Greek biographer of the Roman era, famous for his paired Lives of great Greeks and Romans. His Life of Cæsar follows the soldier and statesman who gave his name to the month of July.
3: Frank A. Haskell (1828–1864) was a Union officer who fought at Gettysburg. His account of The Battle of Gettysburg, written soon after, is a famous firsthand description of the Civil War's turning point.
4: The Declaration of Independence (1776), drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson and adopted by the Continental Congress, announced the American colonies' break from Britain. It sets out the colonists' grievances and their case for self-government.
5: The Thousand and One Nights (the Arabian Nights) is a great medieval collection of Middle Eastern and South Asian tales, told within the frame of Scheherazade's nightly storytelling. Here a tailor spins a tale for a king.
6: Sir Thomas More (1478–1535) was an English statesman, scholar, and saint, Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII. Utopia describes an imaginary island commonwealth and the customs of its people, a book that gave the word “utopia” to the language.
7: Richard Brinsley Sheridan (1751–1816) was an Irish-born playwright and politician, a master of English comedy. The School for Scandal is his comedy of manners set among the gossips and fortune-hunters of fashionable London.
8: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was a leading English Romantic poet. The Cenci is his verse tragedy set in sixteenth-century Italy, drawn from the dark history of a Roman noble family.
9: Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was an English statesman and philosopher who championed the new experimental science. His Essays are brief, pointed reflections on worldly matters; this selection takes up a handful of them.
10: The Voyages to Vinland are episodes from the medieval Icelandic sagas, recounting the Norse seafarers who sailed west from Greenland. They describe the lands these explorers found across the Atlantic, centuries before Columbus.
11: Simon Newcomb (1835–1909) was a Canadian-American astronomer and one of the most celebrated scientists of his day. In The Extent of the Universe he surveys what is known of the size and structure of the cosmos.
12: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was an American essayist and naturalist, author of Walden. Walking is his essay in praise of the wild and of going on foot through the countryside.
13: Plutarch (c. A.D. 46–120) was a Greek biographer of the Roman era, famous for his paired Lives. His Life of Pericles portrays the statesman who led Athens at the height of its golden age.
14: Edmund Burke (1729–1797) was an Irish-born British statesman and philosopher. Reflections on the Revolution in France is his impassioned response, written as the Revolution unfolded, to the upheaval across the Channel.
15: Raphael Holinshed (c. 1525–1580) compiled the great Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland that Shakespeare later drew upon. This passage describes the court and table of Queen Elizabeth's England.
16: The Koran is the sacred scripture of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the word of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad in the seventh century. This selection presents several of its chapters.
17: Jean Racine (1639–1699) was the supreme master of French classical tragedy. Phædra retells the Greek myth of a queen consumed by a forbidden love for her stepson.
18: Robert Browning (1812–1889) was a major English poet of the Victorian age. A Blot in the ’Scutcheon is his verse tragedy of young love, family honor, and a fatal misunderstanding among the English gentry.
19: Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552–1618) was an English courtier, soldier, and explorer of the Elizabethan age. The Discovery of Guiana is his account of his expedition up the Orinoco in search of the fabled golden land of El Dorado.
20: John Bunyan (1628–1688) was an English preacher who wrote his masterpiece while imprisoned for his faith. The Pilgrim's Progress is an allegory in which a man named Christian sets out on a journey toward salvation.
21: Robert Burns (1759–1796) is Scotland's national poet, who wrote in the vivid Scots tongue of country life. This selection gathers a number of his poems.
22: Homer is the traditional author of the ancient Greek epics; the Odyssey recounts the long voyage home of Odysseus after the Trojan War. In this episode he and his men are trapped in the cave of a man-eating giant.
23: Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was an English statesman and philosopher who championed the new experimental science. His Essays are brief, pointed reflections on worldly matters; this selection takes up a handful of them.
24: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was the English naturalist whose later work transformed biology. The Voyage of the Beagle is the journal of his five-year survey expedition; here he records scenes from South America.
25: The Lay of Brynhild is one of the heroic poems of the Old Norse Poetic Edda, preserved in medieval Iceland. It belongs to the legend of Sigurd the dragon-slayer and the warrior-maiden Brynhild.
26: Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-Dutch monk and writer. The Imitation of Christ is his classic of Christian devotion; these short chapters meditate on finding peace amid the strife of life.
27: Joseph Lister (1827–1912) was a British surgeon who pioneered antiseptic surgery. In On the Antiseptic Principle of the Practice of Surgery he reports how guarding wounds against germs transformed the operating room.
28: Abraham Cowley (1618–1667) was an English poet and essayist of the seventeenth century. Of Agriculture is his essay in praise of the country life and the quiet pleasures of working the land.
29: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was the American essayist and lecturer at the heart of New England Transcendentalism. Stonehenge, from his book English Traits, recounts a visit to the ancient stone circle on the English plain.
30: Edward Hayes was an Elizabethan sea captain who sailed with Sir Humphrey Gilbert. His narrative of The Voyage of Sir Humphrey Gilbert recounts the 1583 expedition that claimed Newfoundland for England.
31: Daniel Defoe (c. 1660–1731) was an English writer and journalist, author of Robinson Crusoe. In The Education of Women he argues, well ahead of his time, for giving women a learning equal to men's.
